analysis.one_liner: Repeals the Affordable Care Act and lets only pre-enactment insurance plans keep grandfathered status.
analysis.headline: The bill died in committee: referred to nine House committees on the day it was introduced, given no hearing or vote, and expired when the 114th Congress ended in January 2017.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have repealed the Affordable Care Act in full, effective May 31, 2017, erasing the individual mandate, the employer mandate, Medicaid expansion, and marketplace subsidies. Its main replacement features were narrow: people already enrolled in a health plan when it took effect could keep that plan indefinitely without following ACA rules, and people already on the federal exchange could keep their tax credits. New entrants to the exchanges would have been cut off from premium tax credits, and essential health benefits would be whatever each state required. It also exempted its own budget effects from pay-as-you-go rules.
analysis.who_benefits: People who had a health plan they liked before the repeal date, because they could keep plans that no longer had to cover essential benefits or follow ACA consumer protections. Large employers and insurers also gain by being freed from the employer mandate penalty, coverage reporting, and federal benefit rules. Medical device makers and other businesses gain because the repeal restores the pre-ACA tax code, including repealing ACA-related taxes.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Holders of grandfathered plans, employers, insurers

how_it_helps.text: It repeals the ACA and the health provisions of the 2010 reconciliation act effective May 31, 2017, restoring the laws as if they had never been enacted. [S2] [S3]

Any group plan or insurance a person was enrolled in after the ACA's enactment would become a 'grandfathered health plan' exempt from ACA coverage requirements, with no changes required, and new employees and family members could join such plans. [S3]
People enrolled on the federal exchange who were ineligible for premium tax credits solely because of the Supreme Court's King v. Burwell ruling would be made eligible for the credit. [S2] [S3]
Essential health benefits would be defined by each state rather than by federal rules. [S2] [S3]
The bill exempts its own budgetary effects from the PAYGO scorecards, so its cost to the federal budget would not trigger automatic spending offsets. [S2] [S3]

analysis.who_pays: People with preexisting conditions, because the repeal would erase guaranteed issue and preexisting-condition protections, returning them to a market where insurers could deny or price them out. New enrollees on the exchanges would lose access to premium tax credits, since the credit would be limited to people already enrolled when the bill became law. Millions covered by the Medicaid expansion or marketplace plans without grandfathered status would lose coverage, and everyone with a non-grandfathered plan would lose the ACA's benefit and cost-sharing protections.
analysis.who_pays_short: People with preexisting conditions and new exchange enrollees

drawbacks.text: The bill repeals the entire ACA with no general replacement, so the Medicaid expansion, marketplace subsidies for anyone not already enrolled, and preexisting-condition protections all end on the same date. [S2] [S3]

The premium tax credit would be denied to any health plan unless it covered an individual enrolled through an exchange before the bill's enactment, locking new entrants out of federal premium assistance. [S3]

State-defined essential health benefits mean people in states with minimal requirements could buy plans that omit prescription drugs, maternity care, or mental health coverage, and the repeal restores those gaps nationwide. [S3]
By exempting its budgetary effects from PAYGO scorecards, the bill removes the automatic spending offsets that would normally accompany its multi-hundred-billion-dollar budget impact. [S3]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The protection for people who like their current plan is real but temporary in effect: as those plans turn over and new people need coverage, the market the bill restores is the pre-ACA one, in which insurers could deny coverage or charge more based on health status and federal premium assistance would not be available to new enrollees. A repeal that helps current plan-holders but leaves no coverage pathway for people with preexisting conditions or future applicants concentrates the gains with employers and insurers already in grandfathered plans and pushes the largest risk onto people who get sick or lose employer coverage.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to nine House committees on the day it was introduced and a few subcommittees afterward, but no committee ever acted on it, and it expired when the 114th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative Mario Diaz-Balart introduced the bill on June 18, 2015, with Representative Ileana Ros-Lehtinen as its sole cosponsor. [S3] [S4] [S5]

The same day, the House referred it to the Energy and Commerce, Ways and Means, Education and the Workforce, Natural Resources, Judiciary, House Administration, Rules, Appropriations, and Budget committees. [S5]

In the following weeks it was referred to the Energy and Commerce Health Subcommittee and the Natural Resources Subcommittee on Indian, Insular and Alaska Native Affairs, and no further action was recorded for the rest of the Congress. [S5]
The Congress ended on January 3, 2017, without the bill ever receiving a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote. [S1] [S5]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one had to change anything, because the bill never advanced. The protections and subsidies it would have repealed for people with preexisting conditions and exchange enrollees stayed in place, and the employers and insurers that would have benefited from the repeal of mandates got nothing from this bill. It was a low-cost repeal effort with minimal cosponsor support, and its death reflects that.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: People whose ACA protections stayed in place

against.name: House committee chairs (Energy and Commerce and eight other committees)
against.role: Chairs of the committees to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill, so it sat without action from June 2015 until the Congress ended. [S5]

sides.party_line_note: Both the sponsor and the lone cosponsor were Florida Republicans; no Democrats supported it, and the bill never reached a vote that would have shown a broader split.

industries.note: Repeal frees insurers from federal benefit mandates, coverage reporting, and market rules, but also ends the subsidized exchange marketplace that brought them millions of paying customers; only grandfathered plans and pre-enactment exchange enrollees keep their subsidies. For ordinary people, the same repeal strips preexisting-condition protections and leaves new enrollees without premium assistance.

Repeals the employer mandate penalties for not offering affordable full-time coverage and the associated reporting requirements, directly reducing employer benefit costs at the expense of the coverage mandate. [S2] [S3]

industries.industry: Medical device and other ACA-taxed industries
industries.note: Full repeal restores the pre-ACA tax code, eliminating taxes the ACA imposed on specific industries such as medical devices; the cost is shifted onto the federal budget, which the bill exempts from PAYGO enforcement. [S3]
